data.title: Questioning person to assist in enforcement
data.text:
(1) To enforce or assist in the enforcement of a judgment or order, the Court, on application, may order a person to attend before a person named by the Court to be questioned under oath about a matter in the judgment or order.
(2) The rules related to questioning under Part 5 [Disclosure of Information] apply to questioning conducted in accordance with an order made under this rule.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.29 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: When affidavit of value must be filed
data.text:
Unless the Court otherwise orders, an affidavit of value must be filed before an application is filed for (a) a redemption order, (b) an order that secured property be offered for sale, (c) a foreclosure order, (d) an order confirming sale to the plaintiff or another person, or (e) an order of possession, but not a preservation order.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.30 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

(e) an order of possession, but not a preservation order. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.30 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

Water’s Edge) v. Goertz, [2016] A.J. No. 1195, 2016 ABCA 362 at paras. 27-29 (Alta. C.A.). The court routinely dispenses with affidavits of value at the redemption order stage in foreclosure actions to enforce unpaid condominium contributions. The vast majority of condominium fee foreclosures are resolved without the need to list the property for sale. The priority for a The court assumes that the value of the property exceeds the unpaid contributions for the purposes of setting a redemption period. However, an affidavit of value will be required to set the listing price for the sale.

commentary.text:
The certified copy of title is filed as a stand-alone document, not attached as an exhibit to an affidavit, as contemplated by section 56.4 of the Land Titles Act. R.S.A. 2000 c. L-4. It should be obtained shortly before the hearing, so that the information shown is current.
The copy of title provides proof of registration of the mortgage (or other instrument sued upon) and its priority, the owners of the land, when title was most recently transferred, as well as valuable information about prior and subsequently-registered encumbrances. Records previously filed with the court can fulfil the requirements of this rule.
However, when the foreclosure proceedings stretch over months (or years), a fresh copy of the title is necessary if only to determine whether there are additional subsequent encumbrancers who are entitled to notice and who may have redemption rights.
Note that when a statement of defence has been delivered, rule 7.3 is in play. Therefore, an application for summary judgment is required before seeking final relief (which includes a redemption order determining the validity of the mortgage and the amount due at that time), so the affidavit of default must satisfy both rules 7.3 and 13.18(3). (A review of the plaintiff’s business records is the norm to satisfy the requirement of personal knowledge in foreclosure matters – see the Commentary under rule 13.18(3).) If the mortgage is one of several agreements, it may have to be read “under the shade of the umbrella” agreement, which may mean that there is a triable issue as to its enforceability:
Stankovic v. 1536679 Alberta Ltd.  [2019] A.J. No. 628, 2019 ABCA 187 at para. 48 (Alta. C.A.).

data.title: Offer for sale of secured property
data.text:
(1) The Court may offer secured property for sale at a time and place, in a manner and at a price that the Court considers appropriate.
(2) If the Court orders that secured property be listed with a realtor, a listing agreement approved by the Court must, unless the Court otherwise orders, be appended to, and forms part of, the order granted.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.32 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

This rule provides the court with discretion, along with provisions of the Law of Property Act, to determine the manner of sale of real property in a foreclosure action.
The timing of the sale process is informed by the redemption period granted by the court.

commentary.text:
“Court”, as defined in the Definitions in the , Alberta Rules of Court includes an applications judge and applications judges primarily charged with hearing foreclosure matters. Applications judges, therefore, sometimes consider competing affidavits of value and “determine fair value” for the sale to a plaintiff.
Rule 9.33 guides the process by which a mortgagee may seek to purchase a property that is in foreclosure and permits the mortgagee to bid on a property that has been listed for sale.
An order confirming sale to the plaintiff or other person is achieved through applications within a foreclosure action. When “there is equity in the property, there is a “bias” towards a judicial sale that will generate proceeds for subsequent encumbrancers; foreclosure is treated as the remedy of last resort...”. data.title: Order confirming sale
data.text:
(1) If the Court orders that secured property be offered for sale by tenders filed in Court and a tender is filed, the plaintiff must apply for either or both of the following:
(a) an order confirming sale;
(b) an order rejecting tenders and directing the return of the deposits paid in respect of the rejected tenders.
(2) The application must be scheduled for hearing not more than one month after the date set for the receipt of tenders.
(3) On granting an order confirming sale, the Court may provide any direction that the Court considers appropriate to facilitate closing the sale.
(4) Unless the order states that this subrule does not apply, an order confirming sale must state that the Registrar of Land Titles must not register the order without accompanying evidence of payment of the amount, if any, which the Court orders to be paid, and that evidence may be (a) a certificate of the court clerk that the payment ordered has been paid into Court, or (b) written confirmation by the plaintiff’s lawyer that the plaintiff has received the payment ordered.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.34 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: (1) If the Court orders that secured property be offered for sale by tenders filed in Court and a tender is filed, the plaintiff must apply for either or both of the following:
(a) an order confirming sale
(b) an order rejecting tenders and directing the return of the deposits paid in respect of the rejected tenders.
(2) The application must be scheduled for hearing not more than one month after the date set for the receipt of tenders.
(3) On granting an order confirming sale, the Court may provide any direction that the Court considers appropriate to facilitate closing the sale.

(4) Unless the order states that this subrule does not apply, an order confirming sale must state that the Registrar of Land Titles must not register the order without accompanying evidence of payment of the amount, if any, which the Court orders to be paid, and that evidence may be
(a) a certificate of the court clerk that the payment ordered has been paid into Court, or
(b) written confirmation by the plaintiff’s lawyer that the plaintiff has received the payment ordered. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.34 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
Rule 9.34(4)(b) facilitates the closing of a court-approved sale in a manner similar to a conventional real estate transaction.
Where there are competing tenders, the court will often reject all of them and direct a sealed tender process. After the sealed tenders have been opened, the court will likely accept the best one and will not consider last-minute attempts to increase the offers by unsuccessful tenderers, because doing so would undermine the sealed tender process.
Where the court has granted an order confirming a sale, the terms of the sale are those set out in the order. It is not open to the secured lender simply to agree with the purchaser to change the terms of the sale. The lender must apply to the court on notice to the defendant borrower and subsequent encumbrancers: CIBC v. Mazepa. [2020] A.J. No. 240, 2020 ABQB 147 at paras. 28, 29 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). Contractual terms in a mortgage dealing with the lender taking possession are illegal and unenforceable in Alberta. CIBC v. Mazepa, [2020] A.J. No. 240, 2020 ABQB 147 at paras. 21-23 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). Taking possession without a court order may expose the lender to liability for theft. CIBC v. Mazepa, [2020] A.J. No. 240, 2020 ABQB 147 at para. 26 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
Rule 9.34(3) provides that the court may provide appropriate directions. It is common in foreclosure proceedings for there to be excess funds after the foreclosing mortgagee’s debt and legal costs are paid. Excess funds are routinely directed to be paid into court pending a further application by subsequent encumbrancers and/or the defendant(s), the borrower(s).
Where the borrower applies for the excess funds, the court expects to see evidence that: (a) the borrower is not in bankruptcy, according to the records of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, and was not in bankruptcy when the property was sold (and if the borrower was in bankruptcy, then notice to the trustee in bankruptcy is required); (b) a Personal Property Registry name search of the borrower found no outstanding writs of enforcement; (c) an “actions against” search at the Court of King’s Bench found no outstanding judgments against the borrower; and (d) an historical search of title to the secured property disclosed all encumbrances that were removed by the sale order (and if any were removed, then notice to the encumbrancer is required).

data.title: Checking calculations: assessment of costs and corrections
data.text:
(1) When in a foreclosure action the Court grants an order declaring the balance owing to the plaintiff, an order for sale to the plaintiff or an order confirming sale, or grants judgment against any party, then, before entry of the order, (a) the plaintiff must, unless otherwise ordered by the Court, file and serve on every defendant and subsequent encumbrancer any of the following documents that are applicable:
(i) a statement of the secured indebtedness; (ii) a statement of money received and disbursed in the sale; (iii) a calculation of any deficiency, if a deficiency judgment or declaration of a deficiency is ordered;
PART 9 [Preparation of bill of costs]
(v) the proposed form of order, together with a notice that any defendant and subsequent encumbrancer who considers that any of the applicable documents contains an error may file and serve on the plaintiff a written submission before a date specified in the notice, (b) the assessment officer must assess the reasonable and proper costs under rule 10.41 [Assessment officer’s decision] unless otherwise ordered by the Court, and (c) the assessment officer must (i) check the plaintiff’s calculations, (ii) review any submission by a defendant or subsequent encum- brancer, (iii) correct the amounts in the order, if necessary, (iv) sign the order as court clerk, and (v) return to the plaintiff or the plaintiff’s lawyer the order and a certificate under rule 10.43 .
[Certification of costs payable]
(2) When the order and the certificate have been returned to the plaintiff or the plaintiff’s lawyer, the plaintiff may enter the order and file the certified bill of costs.
(3) If the defendant did not appear at the application for the order and the plaintiff disagrees with (a) the assessment of the reasonable and proper costs, if done without appearance, or (b) the corrections made by the assessment officer under subrule (1)(c)(iii), the plaintiff may, before entry of the order under subrule (2), appear before or speak to the assessment officer to explain the plaintiff’s figures or costs, and the assessment officer may amend or refuse to amend the assessment or correc- tions.
(4) If the plaintiff is not satisfied with the assessment officer’s assessment, whether amended or not, the plaintiff may, before the order is entered, re-attend before the applications judge or judge who granted the order for the purpose of settling the costs or for further directions, at which time the plaintiff must provide to the Court any corrections, bill of costs, notes or other materials from the assessment officer.
(5) To the extent of any inconsistency with Part 10 [Lawyers’ Charges, Recoverable Costs of Litigation, and Sanctions], this rule prevails.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.35 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010); Alta.*

(5) To the extent of any inconsistency with Part 10 [Lawyers’ Charges, Recoverable Costs of Litigation, and Sanctions], this rule prevails. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.35 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)

This rule sets out the process of calculations in relation to foreclosure actions, assessments of costs and corrections. Particularly, rule 9.35(4) permits the plaintiff to reappear and seek to vary the decision of an assessment officer and their assessment of costs. Review of Assessment of Costs – Rule 9.35(4) allows a plaintiff to question an assessment officer’s assessment in a foreclosure action to the applications judge or judge who granted the order. To be open for review, “re-attendance [must] take place before the Order is entered.” Caplink Mortgage Investors Corp. v. Kretschmer, [2012] A.J. No. 637, 2012 ABQB 396 at para. 1 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
As such, orders entered to facilitate the closing of a sale to a third party purchaser will bar the application of rule 9.35(4).

Caplink Mortgage Investors Corp. v. Kretschmer, [2012] A.J. No. 637, 2012 ABQB 396 at para. 1 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). “[T]he determination of the assessment officer, together with the subsequent filing of the Bill of Costs, constitutes the ‘order’ referred to in Rule 9.35(4)”.
Equitable Bank v. Avison, [2015] A.J. No. 166, 2015 ABQB 109 at para. 40 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).

Notice of a rule 9.35(4) application should be provided to the defendant if the defendant appeared at the application where the costs order was granted. Equitable Bank v. Avison, [2015] A.J. No. 166, 2015 ABQB 109 at para. 23 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
Rule 9.35(4) is silent about the nature of the process. Applications judges are not supposed to hear appeals (Court of King’s Bench Act, RSA 2000, c. C-31, section 9(1)(a)(i)).
Paradigm Quest Inc. v. Moser, [2014] A.J. No. 1375, 2014 ABQB 747 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)), revd on other grounds [2015] A.J. No. 1138, 2015 ABQB 557 (Alta. Q.B.).
Accordingly, applications judges should treat rule 9.35(4) as a application and de novo substitute their discretion for the opinion of the assessment officer, if necessary.
Paradigm Quest Inc. v. Moser, [2014] A.J. No. 1375, 2014 ABQB 747 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)), revd on other grounds [2015] A.J. No. 1138, 2015 ABQB 557 (Alta. Q.B.).
An appeal from the review officer’s decision is brought before a judge under rule 10.26.

rules.title: Sale and disposition of land
rules.text:
(1) If land is to be sold, mortgaged, partitioned or exchanged as a result of an action, the Court may make that order and specify the time and place of, the manner of, and the price or sum associated with the transaction that the Court considers appropriate.
(2) If the Court is satisfied that all interested parties are before the Court or bound by the order, the Court may order (a) the sale, mortgage, partition or exchange of land, and (b) the procedure to be carried out to give effect to the order.
(3) Any money produced as a result of carrying out an order under this rule must (a) be paid into Court, (b) be paid to persons specified in the order, or (c) otherwise be dealt with in accordance with the order.
(4) If a judgment or order states that land is to be sold, (a) the sale must be approved by the Court before the sale is completed, and (b) the persons necessary to complete the sale must join the sale and conveyance in accordance with the Court’s order.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.38 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Definitions
sentences: In this Division
(a) “Act” means Part 3 of the International Conventions Implementation Act and includes the Convention
(b) “certified copy” means the original document or a copy of the document certified as being a true copy by the original or facsimile signature of a proper officer of the foreign court

(c) “Convention” means the Convention Between Canada and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland Providing for the Reciprocal Recognition and Enforcement of Judgments in Civil and Commercial Matters in Schedule 3 to the Act

(d) “convention judgment”, “convention judgment creditor”, “conven- tion judgment debtor” and “original court” have the same meanings respectively as “judgment”, “judgment creditor”, “judgment debtor” and “original court” have in the Convention. *[Alta. rules.title: Affidavit in support of application for order to register convention judgment
rules.text:
(1) An originating application for an order to register a convention judgment must be supported by an affidavit (a) stating that the applicant is entitled to enforce the convention judgment and, where applicable, providing full particulars of the entitlement, whether by assignment or otherwise, (b) stating in the original currency of the convention judgment (i) the unpaid balance and interest as of a fixed date that is within 2 months before the date of the originating application, and (ii) the daily interest payable after that fixed date, (c) if applicable, stating the provisions of the convention judgment that are sought to be registered, (d) stating the manner in which the convention judgment debtor submitted to the jurisdiction of the original court, if the convention judgment debtor appeared, defended, attorned or otherwise submit- ted to the jurisdiction of the original court, (e) listing the reasonable costs of and incidental to registration and certifying that the applicant has incurred, is liable to pay or is otherwise entitled to collect them, as the case may be, and (f) containing or to which is attached any other information or document that the Court may require.
(2) The affidavit referred to in subrule (1) must have attached to it (a) a certified copy of the convention judgment and, where applicable, a translation into English authenticated by affidavit or any other method acceptable to the Court, and (b) proof acceptable to the Court that the initiating documents were served on the convention judgment debtor in the original applica- tion, if the convention judgment debtor was served personally with the originating documents in the original action, unless this infor- mation appears in the convention judgment.
(3) An affidavit may contain statements made on the information and belief of the person swearing the affidavit, but must state the source and grounds for the information and belief.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.43 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.text:
(1) On hearing an originating application for an order to register a convention judgment, the Court, after considering the Act, may order that the convention judgment be registered for an amount to be calculated under subrule (2).

Registered in the Court of King’s Bench of Alberta on [date] pursuant to the Order of ______________ dated . . . and (b) filing the order made under subrule (1) and the copy of the convention judgment marked in accordance with clause (a).

commentary.text:
When judgment has been given in a reciprocating jurisdiction, the judgment creditor may apply to the Court of King’s Bench within six years of the date of judgment to register the judgment in the court. Reciprocal Enforcement of Judgments Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. R-6, s. 2(1).
